transcript.en: I copied the same five lines into my program four times, for four classes. Then I found a bug in them, and had to fix it four times. A function would have fixed it once. Today: functions, and how to test them. A function is a named block of code that does one job. You define it once with def, its name, and its inputs, called parameters. Then you call it by name, as often as you like, with different values. Inside a function, return hands a value back to whoever called it. print only shows something on the screen, and the value is lost. If you want to use the answer, in a sum, a test or another function, return it. Variables made inside a function live only inside it, while it runs. That’s called scope. It means a function can’t accidentally change your program’s variables, and you can understand it on its own. Now the engineer’s habit: test every function. An assert line checks that something is true, and stops with an error if it isn’t. Write a few asserts with answers you worked out by hand, including the awkward cases. Quick check! A function prints its answer instead of returning it. You write total equals add of three and four. What is total? None. The seven appears on the screen, but the function gives back nothing, which Python calls None. Use return when the answer is needed later. Use print only to show it to a person. Good functions are small and named for their job. Is leap year, given a year. Grade, given a mark. Total cost, given a price and a number of items. Each one is easy to test on its own. Testing only easy cases proves little. Try the edges: an empty list, a single item, zero, a negative number. An average of an empty list divides by zero. A good test finds that before a user does. In the app, open Step through a program and choose A function. Step through and watch the program jump into area and back. Notice that its own variables exist only while it runs. Your turn. You’ve written average of marks. Which extra test is most useful? The empty list. Remember: a function is a named job, defined once with def and called many times. return hands back a value; print only shows it. Variables inside a function stay inside. And test with assert, edges included. Try it yourself: write a function for something you do often, like working out your average or the cost of a trip. Then write three asserts, including one awkward case, and make them all pass.
transcript.ar: نسخت نفس الخمس سطور في برنامجي أربع مرات، لأربع فصول. وبعدين لقيت فيهم غلطة، واضطريت أصلّحها أربع مرات. لو كانت دالة، كنت صلّحتها مرة واحدة. النهارده: الدوال، وإزاي نختبرها. الدالة حتة كود ليها اسم وبتعمل مهمة واحدة. بتعرّفها مرة واحدة بـ def، واسمها، والمدخلات بتاعتها، اللي اسمها باراميترز. وبعدين بتنادي عليها باسمها، كل ما تحب، بقيم مختلفة. جوّه الدالة، الـ return بترجّع قيمة للي نادى عليها. أما الـ print فبتعرض حاجة على الشاشة وبس، والقيمة بتضيع. لو عايز تستخدم الإجابة، في حساب، أو اختبار، أو دالة تانية، رجّعها بـ return. المتغيّرات اللي بتتعمل جوّه الدالة بتعيش جوّاها بس، وهي شغّالة. ده اسمه النطاق. ومعناه إن الدالة مش هتغيّر متغيّرات برنامجك بالغلط، وإنك تقدر تفهمها لوحدها. ودي بقى عادة المهندسين: اختبر كل دالة. سطر الـ assert بيتأكد إن حاجة صح، ولو مش صح بيقف برسالة خطأ. اكتب كام assert بإجابات حسبتها بإيدك، ومنهم الحالات الصعبة. سؤال سريع! دالة بتطبع الإجابة بدل ما ترجّعها. كتبت total يساوي add لتلاتة وأربعة. total هتبقى كام؟ None. السبعة بتظهر على الشاشة، بس الدالة مابترجّعش حاجة، وبايثون بيسمّي ده None. استخدم return لما الإجابة هتلزم بعدين. واستخدم print بس علشان تعرضها لإنسان. الدوال الكويسة صغيرة واسمها على مهمتها. is leap year، بتاخد سنة. وgrade، بتاخد درجة. وtotal cost، بتاخد سعر وعدد حاجات. وكل واحدة سهل تختبرها لوحدها. إنك تختبر الحالات السهلة بس مابيثبتش كتير. جرّب الأطراف: ليست فاضية، وعنصر واحد، وصفر، ورقم سالب. متوسط ليست فاضية بيقسم على صفر. والاختبار الكويس بيلاقي ده قبل ما المستخدم يلاقيه. في التطبيق، افتح «تتبّع البرنامج خطوة بخطوة» واختار «دالة». اتتبّعه واتفرّج على البرنامج وهو بينط جوّه الدالة area ويرجع. وخد بالك إن متغيّراتها الخاصة موجودة بس وهي شغّالة. دورك. كتبت دالة average للدرجات. أنهي اختبار زيادة أنفع؟ الليست الفاضية. افتكر: الدالة مهمة ليها اسم، بتتعرّف مرة بـ def وبتتنادي مرات كتير. الـ return بترجّع قيمة، والـ print بتعرضها بس. والمتغيّرات اللي جوّه الدالة بتفضل جوّاها. واختبر بـ assert، ومعاها الأطراف. جرّبها بنفسك: اكتب دالة لحاجة بتعملها كتير، زي إنك تحسب متوسطك أو تكلفة مشوار. وبعدين اكتب تلات assert، منهم حالة صعبة، وخلّيهم كلهم ينجحوا.

body.en:
When the same few lines appear in four places, a bug has to be fixed four times. A function gives those lines a name, so you write them once and call them wherever you need them. def area(length, width): starts a function; length and width are its parameters, the values it needs. area(4, 3) calls it with the arguments 4 and 3.

return hands a result back to the line that called the function: room = area(4, 3) stores 12. print only shows something on the screen; the value is then lost. A function that prints instead of returning can’t be used in a sum, and gives back None. Variables made inside a function are its own: they exist only while it runs.

Functions are easy to test. assert average([10, 12, 14]) == 12 stops the program with an AssertionError if the answer is wrong, and does nothing if it is right. Write a few asserts for each function, including the edge cases: an empty list, a single item, negative numbers. What should average([]) give? Deciding that is part of designing the function.

Good functions do one job, have a name that says what it is, and return their result rather than printing it.

حين تظهر الأسطر القليلة نفسها في أربعة أماكن، يجب أن يُصلح الخطأ أربع مرات. أمّا الدالة فتعطي تلك الأسطر اسمًا، فتكتبها مرة واحدة وتستدعيها حيثما احتجت إليها. يبدأ السطر ⁦def area(length, width)⁩: دالة، وlength وwidth معاملاتها، أي القيم التي تحتاج إليها. وتستدعيها ⁦area(4, 3)⁩ بالقيمتين 4 و3.

تعيد return نتيجةً إلى السطر الذي استدعى الدالة: فـ ⁦room = area(4, 3)⁩ تخزّن 12. أمّا print فتُظهر شيئًا على الشاشة فقط، ثم تضيع القيمة. والدالة التي تطبع بدل أن تعيد لا يمكن استعمالها في عملية حسابية، وتعيد None. والمتغيّرات التي تُنشأ داخل الدالة خاصّة بها: لا توجد إلّا أثناء عملها.

واختبار الدوال سهل. فالسطر ⁦assert average([10, 12, 14]) == 12⁩ يوقف البرنامج برسالة AssertionError إن كان الجواب خاطئًا، ولا يفعل شيئًا إن كان صحيحًا. اكتب بضعة أسطر assert لكل دالة، ومعها الحالات الحدّية: قائمة فارغة، وعنصر واحد، وأعداد سالبة. ماذا يجب أن تعطي ⁦average([])⁩؟ تقرير ذلك جزء من تصميم الدالة.

والدالة الجيدة تؤدّي مهمة واحدة، ولها اسم يقول ما هي، وتعيد نتيجتها بدل أن تطبعها.

transcript.en: Our school weather station logs a temperature every hour: twenty-four numbers a day. What was the hottest hour? How many hours were above thirty? A list and a loop answer both. Today: lists and loops together. A list keeps values in order. Positions count from zero, so temps at zero is the first reading. Negative positions count from the end: temps at minus one is the last. len tells you how many there are. append adds a reading to the end. A slice takes part of a list: temps from one to three gives the items at one and two, stopping before three, just like range. The list itself isn’t changed. Python has max, but writing it yourself teaches the pattern. Start with the first item as the best so far. Loop over the rest, and whenever one is bigger, keep it instead. At the end, best is the largest. The same loop can count and total. Add one to a count whenever a reading passes a test. Add every reading to a total. Then total divided by the length is the average. Three patterns, one loop. Quick check! The list is twenty-one, twenty-five, thirty-one, twenty-eight. What is temps at minus one? Twenty-eight, the last reading. And temps at four would stop the program with an IndexError: four items have positions zero to three. Most list bugs are off by one. A list can also act as a stack or a queue. append adds to the end. pop takes from the end, last in, first out: that’s a stack, like undo. pop of zero takes from the front, first in, first out: that’s a queue. Lists are everywhere in real programs. A playlist is a list of songs. A class register is a list of names. A sensor log is a list of readings. And your phone’s messages are a list, newest last. In the app, open Stacks and queues. Type three words, make one bold, then press Undo twice: a stack. Then let four customers into the queue and serve two: the first to arrive are served first. Your turn. A loop adds one to hot whenever a reading is above thirty. For twenty-one, thirty-one, thirty-five and thirty, what is hot? Two. Remember: positions count from zero, and minus one is the last. A loop can find the largest, count and total in one pass. append adds; pop takes. And check the boundaries, like exactly thirty. Try it yourself: for one week, write down how many minutes you spend on your phone each day. Put the seven numbers in a list, and write a program for the total, the average and the biggest day.

body.en:
A list holds many values in order: temps = [21, 25, 31, 28]. Each has an index, counting from 0, so temps[0] is 21. Negative indexes count from the end: temps[-1] is the last item. A slice takes a part: temps[1:3] is [25, 31], from index 1 up to, but not including, 3. temps.append(30) adds to the end, and len(temps) says how many there are. Asking for temps[4] in a list of four is an IndexError.

Loops over lists answer most questions about data. for t in temps: visits every value. A counter (hot = hot + 1 when t > 30) counts; a running total adds; and the largest value so far finds the maximum without max(): start with the first item and replace it whenever you meet a bigger one. Starting at 0 instead would fail on a list of negative temperatures.

Lists can also behave as two classic structures. A stack is last in, first out, like a pile of plates or the undo button: append to add, pop() to take the newest. A queue is first in, first out, like the canteen line: append to join, pop(0) to serve the first.

transcript.en: The exam office has a thousand candidates in a sorted list, and a student asks: am I on it? Checking every name could take a thousand looks. There’s a way that needs only ten. Today: searching, one by one or by halving. Linear search checks each item in turn, from the start. It works on any list, sorted or not. If the item is found, return its position; if the loop ends without finding it, return minus one. How much work is that? If the item is last, or missing, linear search looks at every item. For a thousand names, that’s a thousand comparisons. For a million, a million. The work grows in step with the list. Binary search is cleverer, but it needs a sorted list. Look at the middle item. If it’s what you want, stop. If your target is bigger, throw away the lower half; if smaller, the upper half. Repeat on what’s left. Each step halves what’s left. A thousand, five hundred, two hundred and fifty, and so on: about ten steps to reach one. A million needs only about twenty. That’s why dictionaries and contact lists are kept in order. Quick check! Which list can binary search use: the names in the order pupils arrived, or the names in alphabetical order? The alphabetical list. Binary search throws half away on every step, and that’s only safe if the list is sorted. On an unsorted list, it can miss a name that’s really there. In code, keep two markers, lo and hi, around the part that’s left. Each time round, look at the middle. Move lo up or hi down. When lo passes hi, the target isn’t there. So which should you use? body.en:
Searching means finding one item among many. Linear search checks the items one by one from the start, and returns the position as soon as it finds the target, or -1 if it reaches the end. It works on any list, sorted or not. In the worst case, when the target is last or missing, it looks at every item: 1,000 looks for 1,000 names.

Binary search is much faster, but only on a sorted list. Look at the middle item. If it is the target, stop. If the target is bigger, it can only be in the right half, so throw the left half away; if smaller, throw the right half away. Each look halves what is left, so 1,000 names need at most about 10 looks, and a million about 20. It needs two markers, lo and hi, for the part still possible, and the loop runs while lo <= hi.

Python has searching built in: x in names and names.index(x) are linear searches. That’s fine for a class list. For big data, keep it sorted and halve, or use a set or dictionary, which find items in about one step.

البحث هو إيجاد عنصر واحد بين عناصر كثيرة. فالبحث الخطّي يفحص العناصر واحدًا واحدًا من البداية، ويعيد الموضع فور إيجاد الهدف، أو -1 إن وصل إلى النهاية. وهو يعمل على أيّ قائمة، مرتّبة أو غير مرتّبة. وفي أسوأ حالة، حين يكون الهدف الأخير أو غير موجود، ينظر إلى كل عنصر: ١٠٠٠ نظرة لـ ١٠٠٠ اسم.

transcript.en: Sports day results came in a heap of a hundred times, in no order. Two students sorted them in two different ways. Both got it right, but one did ten times the work. Today: sorting, and how to judge an algorithm. Bubble sort is the simplest. Compare each pair of neighbours, and swap them if they’re in the wrong order. After one pass, the biggest value has bubbled to the end. Repeat until a pass makes no swaps. Insertion sort works like sorting cards in your hand. Take the next card, and slide it left past every bigger one until it fits. On a list that’s nearly sorted, almost nothing has to move, so it’s very fast. Merge sort is cleverer. Split the list in half, sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves by taking the smaller front item each time. For big lists it does far less work than bubble or insertion sort. To compare algorithms fairly, count their steps, not the seconds on one phone. Bubble sort on n items does about n times n, divided by two, comparisons. Merge sort does about n times log n. For a thousand items, that’s about half a million against about ten thousand. Quick check! A list of marks is already sorted, except two neighbours swapped. Which sort finishes with the fewest steps? Judge an algorithm by correctness first. Test it on the edge cases: an empty list, one item, a list already sorted, a list in reverse, and repeated values. You can even let the computer check. A function, is sorted, walks through the list and compares each item with the next. If any pair is in the wrong order, the list isn’t sorted. Run it after every sort you write. body.en:
Sorting puts items in order, and there are many algorithms for it. Bubble sort compares each pair of neighbours and swaps them if they are in the wrong order; after one pass the biggest value has “bubbled” to the end, and it repeats until a pass makes no swaps. Insertion sort works like sorting cards in your hand: take the next card and slide it left past every bigger one. Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item.

To compare algorithms fairly, count their steps, not the seconds on one phone. Bubble and insertion sort make up to about n × n ÷ 2 comparisons on a mixed-up list; merge sort about n × log n. For 1,000 items that is roughly half a million against about ten thousand. But the data matters: on a nearly sorted list, insertion sort barely moves anything. Python’s sorted() uses a clever mix, and is the one to use in real programs.

Speed means nothing if the answer is wrong. Judge an algorithm by correctness first: test it on the edge cases (an empty list, one item, a list already sorted, a list in reverse, repeated values) and check the result with a function such as is_sorted.

يضع الترتيب العناصر بترتيبها، وله خوارزميات كثيرة. فالترتيب الفقاعي يقارن كل زوج متجاور ويبدّلهما إن كانا في غير ترتيبهما، وبعد دورة واحدة «تطفو» القيمة الكبرى إلى النهاية، ويكرّر حتى تمرّ دورة بلا تبديل. والترتيب بالإدراج يعمل مثل ترتيب الأوراق في يدك: خذ الورقة التالية وحرّكها إلى اليسار متجاوزًا كل ورقة أكبر منها. والترتيب بالدمج يقسم القائمة نصفين، ويرتّب كل نصف، ثم يدمج النصفين المرتّبين بأخذ العنصر الأصغر من مقدّمتيهما مرة بعد مرة.

ولكي تقارن الخوارزميات بإنصاف، عُدّ خطواتها لا الثواني على هاتف واحد. فالترتيب الفقاعي والترتيب بالإدراج يقومان بما يصل إلى نحو ⁦n × n ÷ 2⁩ مقارنة على قائمة مختلطة، والترتيب بالدمج بنحو ⁦n × log n⁩. ولـ ١٠٠٠ عنصر يعني ذلك نحو نصف مليون مقابل نحو عشرة آلاف. لكن البيانات مهمة: ففي قائمة شبه مرتّبة لا يكاد الترتيب بالإدراج يحرّك شيئًا. وتستعمل ⁦sorted()⁩ في Python مزيجًا ذكيًا، وهي التي تُستعمل في البرامج الحقيقية.

ولا معنى للسرعة إن كان الجواب خاطئًا. احكم على الخوارزمية بصحّتها أولًا: اختبرها على الحالات الحدّية (قائمة فارغة، وعنصر واحد، وقائمة مرتّبة أصلًا، وقائمة معكوسة، وقيم متكرّرة)، وتحقّق من النتيجة بدالة مثل is_sorted.

Bubble (7 min): Walk along the row comparing neighbours; swap any pair in the wrong order. Repeat passes until no swaps. Record the comparisons.
Insertion (7 min): Mix the row again the same way. Take each person in turn and slide them left past everyone bigger. Record the comparisons.

explain.en: f(3) returns 6, so f(3) + 1 is 7. Because f returns its result, it can be used in a sum.

prompt.ar: اكتب ⁦count_above(values, limit)⁩: تعيد عدد القيم الأكبر من limit.

hint.en: Use limit, not a fixed number.

tests.check: assert count_above([], 5) == 0, "an empty list has none"

hints.en: count = 0; for v in values: if v > limit: count = count + 1; return count.
hints.ar: ⁦count = 0⁩، ثم ⁦for v in values: if v > limit: count = count + 1⁩، ثم return count.

explain.en: A counter in a loop, returned after the loop. > leaves the limit itself out, and the empty list gives 0 without any special case.
explain.ar: عدّاد في حلقة يُعاد بعدها. وتستثني > الحدّ نفسه، وتعطي القائمة الفارغة 0 دون حالة خاصة.

prompt.en: total should return the sum of the list, but for [4, 6, 8] it returns 4. Which line is wrong?
prompt.ar: يجب أن تعيد total مجموع القائمة، لكنها تعيد 4 للقائمة ⁦[4, 6, 8]⁩. أيّ سطر فيه الخطأ؟

explain.en: The return is indented inside the loop, so the function returns after the first item. Moving it back one level returns after the loop has finished.
explain.ar: سطر return مُزاح داخل الحلقة، فتعود الدالة بعد العنصر الأول. وإرجاعه مستوى واحدًا يجعلها تعود بعد انتهاء الحلقة.

explain.en: n, log n, n × n and n × log n: the same 1,000 items, very different amounts of work.
explain.ar: n وlog n و⁦n × n⁩ و⁦n × log n⁩: العناصر الألف نفسها، ومقادير مختلفة جدًا من العمل.

explain.en: Halving a million reaches 1 in about 20 steps. Linear search could need all million.
explain.ar: تنصيف المليون يصل إلى ١ في نحو ٢٠ خطوة. أمّا البحث الخطّي فقد يحتاج إلى المليون كله.

explain.en: A stack takes from the end: pop() gives the last item added, B. pop(0) takes from the front, which is how a queue works, and would give A.
explain.ar: يأخذ المكدّس من النهاية: تعطي ⁦pop()⁩ آخر عنصر أُضيف، B. أمّا ⁦pop(0)⁩ فتأخذ من البداية، كما يعمل الطابور، وستعطي A.

explain.en: Empty, single and repeated values are where sorts break. Another random list tests nothing new.

prompt.en: Fill the gaps: last is the last reading, and first_two the first two.
prompt.ar: املأ الفراغات: last هي القراءة الأخيرة، وfirst_two القراءتان الأوليان.

explain.en: -1 counts from the end; a slice from 0 up to, but not including, 2 gives the first two. temps[4] would be an IndexError.
explain.ar: -1 تعدّ من النهاية، والشريحة من 0 حتى 2 دون أن تشملها تعطي العنصرين الأولين. أمّا ⁦temps[4]⁩ فتسبّب IndexError.

body.en:
Write a Python program of your own, built from small functions that each do one job, that works with a list of real data: your class marks, a week of weather readings or a shop's prices. It must search or sort the data and you must test each function.

You've already started. The projects in this course's four lessons are your milestones: reuse what you made there.
1. Functions: one job each: A tested toolkit
2. Lists and loops: A week of readings
3. Searching: The search race
4. Sorting, and judging algorithms: Sort and prove it

Pick one idea, or bring your own:
- A marks report: average, top three, who improved
- A weather week: hottest day, sorted readings
- A price finder: cheapest shop for each item

Then send three things: your work, an explanation of how it works in your own words, and an honest note on whether you used AI. Your explanation matters most: it shows you understand what you built. Using AI is allowed if you say how, and the explanation must still be yours. Nothing here is marked: your teacher reads it to see what you understand.
body.ar:
اكتب برنامج بايثون من عندك، متقسّم لدوال صغيرة كل واحدة بتعمل حاجة واحدة، وبيشتغل على قايمة بيانات حقيقية: درجات فصلك، أو قراءات الجو في أسبوع، أو أسعار محل. لازم يدوّر في البيانات أو يرتّبها، ولازم تختبر كل دالة.

انت بدأت خلاص. مشاريع الأربع دروس اللي في الكورس ده هي المراحل بتاعتك: استخدم اللي عملته فيها.
1. الدوال: لكل دالة مهمة: عُدّة مختبَرة
2. القوائم والحلقات: أسبوع من القراءات
3. البحث: سباق البحث
4. الترتيب والحكم على الخوارزميات: رتّب وأثبت

اختار فكرة من دول، أو هات فكرتك انت:
- تقرير درجات: المتوسط، وأعلى تلاتة، ومين اتحسّن
- أسبوع جو: أحرّ يوم، والقراءات مترتبة
- دوّار الأسعار: أرخص محل لكل حاجة

وبعدين ابعت تلات حاجات: شغلك، وشرح بكلامك انت لإزاي بيشتغل، وكلمة صريحة عن هل استخدمت ذكاء اصطناعي ولا لأ. الشرح هو أهم حاجة: بيبيّن إنك فاهم اللي عملته. استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي مسموح لو قلت استخدمته إزاي، بس الشرح لازم يبقى بتاعك انت. مفيش درجات هنا: مدرّسك بيقرا شغلك عشان يشوف انت فاهم إيه.
